title: The written code
hookLine: the Sikh Rehat Maryada, agreed by the panth in the 1940s and published in 1950, sets out the shared code

cards: Every family has rules nobody wrote down. Shoes off at the door. Grandma gets the first plate.
Nobody touches the remote during the cricket. They work fine until the family grows, moves across three continents, and the cousins start arguing about what the rule actually was.
Then somebody says: we should write this down. The Sikh panth reached that moment in the twentieth century, spread from Punjab to Malaya to California. Today: the written code.

teach.h: MARYADA — THE AGREED WAY, THE BOUNDARY.
teach.b: Rehat, from the start of this stretch, is the way a Sikh lives. Maryada means a boundary, a proper limit, the accepted way things are done. So Rehat Maryada is the agreed shape of a Sikh life.
In the eighteenth century there were rahitnamas, manuals of conduct linked by tradition to the Guru's companions, and they didn't always agree.
So in the 1930s, the SGPC, the elected body that runs the historic gurdwaras, gathered scholars and community leaders to version one shared code. It took years of meetings and versions.
The panth agreed it in the 1940s, and it was published in 1950. It's short enough to read in an evening, and it has two halves.

teach.h: PERSONAL LIFE, AND THE COMMUNITY'S LIFE.
teach.b: One is personal life: meditating on the Name, the daily prayers morning, evening and night, living by the Guru's teaching, honest work, sharing, service.
The other is the community's life: how a gurdwara runs, how the Guru Granth Sahib is honored, the ceremonies for birth, naming, marriage and death, amrit, and how the panth decides things together.
Everything in this stretch lives in it: kesh, kangha, kara, kachhera, kirpan, the four things avoided, the step of amrit, and yesterday's definition of a Sikh.
The code isn't the Guru. For Sikhs, the Guru is the Guru Granth Sahib; the Rehat Maryada is the family agreement about how to live around the Guru. And it's shared.
Some Sikh groups keep their own maryada alongside it, or instead. But a Sikh in Toronto and a Sikh in Amritsar can open the same short book and read the same words.

how: The Sikh Rehat Maryada, published by the SGPC, is used by gurdwaras in India and abroad to guide worship and ceremonies; Sikhs preparing for amrit often read it.

practice: Here's one line from the code, in plain words: a Sikh should earn by honest work, and share with others.
Say it to yourself once, slowly, then think back over this stretch, from the hair kept to the open door, and hold whichever one stayed with you.
